course: Petrol and Diesel Engine Fundamentals: 0 to 12 Litres

lessons.title: Heavy-Duty Truck and Bus Diesel Engines
lessons.body:
Heavy-duty truck and bus diesel engines in the 6 to 12 litre range are the workhorses of African transport. Common models include the Cummins ISX (10.8L), Mercedes-Benz OM 501 (12L), and Toyota 1HZ (4.2L but often used in buses). These engines run on diesel, use direct injection, and often have turbochargers. They produce high torque at low RPM, ideal for hauling loads on rough roads.

In Africa, these engines face dusty conditions, poor fuel quality, and long hours. Regular maintenance is critical. For example, a Cummins ISX needs oil changes every 15,000 km or 500 hours, whichever comes first. Use API CJ-4 or better oil. Fuel filters must be changed every 10,000 km because dirty diesel clogs injectors. A common problem is worn injector tips causing black smoke and power loss. Testing injectors requires a pop tester or a diagnostic scanner.

Tools you need: a 3/4-inch drive socket set, torque wrench (up to 300 Nm), fuel pressure gauge, and a multimeter. When checking valve clearance on a cold engine, set intake to 0.30 mm and exhaust to 0.50 mm for many models. Adjust with a feeler gauge and screwdriver.

If the engine overheats, check the thermostat and radiator cap first. In African heat, a 50/50 coolant mix is essential. Also, check the fan clutch â if it spins freely when hot, replace it. For hard starting, test glow plugs (if fitted) or grid heater. A weak battery can also cause slow cranking; load test it.

Fuel savings tip: keep tyres inflated to recommended pressure (e.g., 110 psi for truck tyres). A soft tyre increases fuel use by 5%. Also, avoid idling for more than 5 minutes. Idling burns 1 litre per hour. For buses, ensure the air filter is clean â a clogged filter can increase fuel consumption by 10%. Use a restriction gauge to check.

When rebuilding, always replace head bolts â they are torque-to-yield. Torque in three steps: 50 Nm, 100 Nm, then 90 degrees. Use a dial indicator to check liner protrusion; it should be 0.05â0.15 mm. If not, shim the liners. These engines can last 1,000,000 km if maintained well.

lessons.title: Construction and Mining Equipment Engines
lessons.body:
Construction and mining equipment like excavators, bulldozers, and loaders use diesel engines from 6 to 12 litres. Examples: Caterpillar C9 (8.8L), Komatsu SAA6D125E (11.1L), and Volvo D12 (12L). These engines work in extreme dust, heat, and vibration. They often run at high load for hours. Maintenance must be proactive.

Key difference from truck engines: these have heavy-duty cooling systems and multi-stage air filters. The air filter has a primary and safety element. Clean the primary by blowing compressed air from inside out, but never clean the safety element â replace it. In dusty mines, check the dust bowl daily. A clogged filter causes power loss and black smoke.

Fuel system: common rail or unit injectors. Water in fuel is a killer. Install a water separator and drain it daily. If you see water in the bowl, drain until diesel flows. Replace fuel filters every 500 hours. Use a filter wrench â not a screwdriver â to avoid damage.

Oil analysis is your best friend. Take a sample every 250 hours. If you see high iron, it means cylinder wear. High copper indicates bearing wear. Change oil every 500 hours with API CI-4 or CH-4. For mining, use oil with high TBN (total base number) to neutralise acids.

Hydraulic systems often share the engine's cooling. Check hydraulic oil level daily. If the engine overheats, the hydraulic oil cooler might be clogged. Clean with compressed air or water. Also, check the radiator for dust build-up â blow it out weekly.

Starting problems: check battery voltage (should be 24V for most). If it cranks slowly, clean battery terminals and check earth straps. In cold conditions, use a block heater or ether starting aid â but use ether sparingly, as it can damage pistons.

When replacing a turbocharger, always pre-lube the oil inlet with clean oil. Check for play in the shaft â if it moves more than 0.1 mm side-to-side, replace. After fitting, run the engine at idle for 2 minutes before revving to circulate oil.

For undercarriage, engine power loss often comes from a clogged aftercooler. Remove and clean with a degreaser. Also, check for boost leaks â a loose clamp can cause low power. Use a soapy water spray to find leaks.

Remember: these engines are expensive. A rebuilt C9 can cost $10,000. So follow the manual. Keep a logbook of hours and maintenance. Train your operators to do daily checks: oil, coolant, fuel, and air filter. That prevents 80% of breakdowns.

lessons.title: Marine Diesel Engines up to 12 Litres
lessons.body:
Marine diesel engines up to 12 litres power fishing boats, ferries, and small cargo vessels. Common models: Yanmar 6LY (5.8L), Cummins QSB6.7 (6.7L), and Volvo Penta D6 (5.5L). These are often based on industrial engines but have marine-specific parts: raw water pump, heat exchanger, and wet exhaust. They run at continuous high load and face saltwater corrosion.

Cooling system: raw water (seawater) is pumped through a heat exchanger to cool the closed-loop freshwater. The raw water pump impeller is rubber and must be replaced every 500 hours or annually. If it fails, the engine overheats fast. Always carry a spare impeller and a pump puller. Check the heat exchanger for zinc anodes â replace them every 6 months. If anodes are gone, the exchanger corrodes and leaks.

Fuel system: marine diesel often has water contamination. Use a primary filter with a water separator and a secondary filter. Drain water daily. Bleed the system after filter change: open the bleed screw on the filter housing and pump the primer until bubble-free fuel comes out. Then bleed at the injection pump.

Exhaust: wet exhaust mixes cooling water with exhaust gases. If you see steam instead of water, the impeller is likely bad. Also, check the exhaust elbow for carbon build-up â clean it yearly. A clogged elbow causes back pressure and power loss.

Corrosion protection: spray all electrical connectors with silicone spray. Use dielectric grease on battery terminals. Check engine mounts â rubber degrades in salt air. If mounts are soft, replace them.

Oil: use marine-grade diesel oil (API CF or higher). Change every 250 hours. Check oil level daily â if it rises, you may have fuel dilution from a leaking injector. If it falls, check for leaks.

Winterizing: in cold climates, drain raw water system or add antifreeze. In Africa, this is less critical, but if the boat is unused for months, fog the engine with oil.

Common problems: overheating at high RPM â check raw water strainer. If clogged with seaweed, clean it. Also, check the thermostat â marine thermostats often fail open, causing cold running and carbon build-up.

Transmission: marine gearboxes use ATF or engine oil. Check level with engine idling in neutral. Change every 500 hours. If the gear slips, check cable adjustment first.

When buying a used marine engine, do a compression test. Remove injectors and use a diesel compression gauge. Minimum compression for a 6L engine is about 25 bar. If low, it needs overhaul. Also, check for rust in the intake â a sign of water ingress.

Safety: always ventilate the engine room before starting. Diesel fumes can explode. Keep a CO2 extinguisher on board. And never run the engine with the raw water seacock closed â you'll burn the impeller in seconds.

lessons.title: High-Performance Petrol Engines
lessons.body:
High-performance petrol engines in the 6 to 12 litre range are rare but exist in muscle cars, race trucks, and some SUVs. Examples: Dodge Viper 8.4L V10, Chevrolet LS7 7.0L V8, and Ford Godzilla 7.3L V8. In Africa, you might find these in imported performance vehicles or modified off-roaders. They use port fuel injection or direct injection, high compression, and variable valve timing.

These engines need high-octane petrol (95 RON or higher). Using low-octane fuel causes knock, which can destroy pistons. If you hear pinging under load, retard timing or use octane booster. In many African countries, 95 is available, but check.

Oil: use full synthetic 5W-30 or 10W-40 with API SN or higher. Change every 10,000 km. For track use, change every 5,000 km. High RPM causes oil shear, so use a quality filter with anti-drainback valve.

Spark plugs: iridium or platinum, gapped to 1.1 mm. Replace every 60,000 km. If you see black soot, the engine is running rich. If white, it's lean â check fuel pressure. A lean condition can melt pistons.

Cooling: these engines produce high heat. Use a 50/50 coolant mix. Check radiator hoses for softness. Replace the thermostat every 5 years. If overheating, check the water pump â often driven by the serpentine belt. A failing pump leaks from the weep hole.

Fuel system: direct injection engines have high-pressure pumps (up to 200 bar). Never open the fuel lines while running. If you suspect a clogged injector, use a fuel injector cleaner in the tank. For port injection, clean the MAF sensor with MAF cleaner â don't touch the wire.

Tuning: many owners add cold air intakes and exhausts. That's fine, but without a tune, you may run lean. Use a handheld tuner or visit a dyno. A wideband O2 sensor gauge helps monitor air/fuel ratio. Target 12.5:1 at wide-open throttle for best power.

Common problems: LS engines suffer from lifter failure if oil is dirty. Viper V10s can have valve guide wear. Godzilla 7.3L is reliable but needs good oil. Always use a torque wrench on spark plugs â aluminium heads strip easily. Torque to 25 Nm.

If the engine misfires, scan for codes. P0300 means random misfire â check plugs, coils, and injectors. Swap coils to see if misfire moves. A compression test should show 10â12 bar. If low, do a leak-down test.

For off-road use, protect the engine from dust. Use a snorkel and a pre-filter. Change air filter every 10,000 km in dusty conditions. Also, ensure the radiator is clean â mud reduces cooling.

These engines are fun but thirsty. Expect 15â20 L/100 km. To save fuel, keep RPM below 2,500 and avoid hard acceleration. But if you want performance, you pay at the pump.

lessons.title: Fuel Efficiency and Emission Strategies
lessons.body:
Large displacement engines (6â12L) consume a lot of fuel. In Africa, where fuel costs are high, efficiency matters. This lesson covers practical strategies to reduce fuel use and emissions without sacrificing reliability.

First, driving habits. For trucks and buses, keep RPM in the sweet spot â usually 1,200â1,800 RPM for diesel. Use the highest gear possible without lugging. Avoid aggressive acceleration; it can increase fuel use by 20%. Use cruise control on highways. For petrol engines, shift up early â around 2,000 RPM. Avoid idling: a 10-litre diesel idles at about 2 litres per hour. Turn it off if parked for more than 5 minutes.

Second, maintenance. A clogged air filter increases fuel consumption by up to 10%. Check it monthly. Under-inflated tyres increase rolling resistance â check weekly. A wheel alignment issue can cost 5% fuel. Use low-viscosity engine oil (e.g., 5W-30 instead of 15W-40) for a 2% saving. But ensure it meets the API rating. Replace fuel filters regularly â dirty injectors waste fuel.

Third, aerodynamics. For trucks, add a roof fairing and side skirts. These can improve fuel economy by 10â15% at highway speeds. Keep the trailer gap tight. For buses, smooth bodywork helps.

Fourth, emissions. Diesel engines produce NOx and particulate matter (PM). To reduce PM, ensure proper combustion â check injection timing. Retarded timing reduces NOx but increases PM. Use a diesel particulate filter (DPF) if fitted. In Africa, many engines don't have DPF, so use low-sulphur diesel (50 ppm or less). If not available, change oil more often.

For petrol engines, catalytic converters reduce CO and HC. If your vehicle has one, use unleaded petrol only. Leaded petrol destroys the catalyst. Also, keep the O2 sensor working â a bad sensor increases fuel use by 15%.

Fifth, alternative strategies. For fleets, use telematics to monitor idling, harsh braking, and speeding. Train drivers. A good driver can save 10% fuel. Also, plan routes to avoid traffic and hills. Use GPS.

Finally, consider retrofits. For older diesel engines, adding a turbocharger or intercooler can improve efficiency. But ensure the fuel pump is calibrated. For petrol, a proper tune-up can restore power and economy.

Remember: fuel savings of 10% on a truck using 30 L/100 km saves 3 litres per 100 km. At $1.50 per litre, that's $4.50 per 100 km. Over 100,000 km, that's $4,500. Worth the effort.

Also, emissions affect health. In cities, diesel soot causes respiratory problems. Keep your engine well-tuned. If you see black smoke, fix it. It's wasting fuel and harming people.

lessons.title: Preventive Maintenance Schedules
lessons.body:
Preventive maintenance (PM) is the key to long engine life. For 6â12 litre engines, follow a schedule based on hours or kilometres. This lesson gives a practical schedule for trucks, construction, and marine. Always refer to your owner's manual, but these are general guidelines.

Daily checks: before starting, check engine oil level (dipstick), coolant level (cold), and fuel level. Drain water from fuel filter. Check for leaks under the engine. Look at belts for cracks. Check tyre pressure (trucks) or raw water strainer (marine). This takes 10 minutes and prevents breakdowns.

Every 250 hours or 10,000 km (whichever first): change engine oil and filter. For diesel, use API CI-4 or CJ-4. For petrol, API SN. Also, check air filter â clean or replace if dirty. Check battery electrolyte level (if serviceable) and terminals. Lubricate chassis and driveline. Inspect coolant hoses.

Every 500 hours or 20,000 km: replace fuel filters (both primary and secondary). Check valve clearance â adjust if noisy. Inspect turbocharger for play and oil leaks. Check injector return flow. For marine, replace raw water impeller. For construction, check hydraulic oil level and filter.

Every 1,000 hours or 40,000 km: change transmission fluid and filter. Change differential oil. Flush cooling system and replace coolant. Replace air filter element (not just clean). Check and adjust belts. Inspect engine mounts. For diesel, check injection timing. For petrol, replace spark plugs (iridium every 60,000 km, but check earlier).

Every 2,000 hours or 80,000 km: replace timing belt (if equipped) or inspect timing chain. Replace water pump if leaking. Check and replace thermostat. Service turbocharger (clean vanes). Replace glow plugs (diesel). For marine, replace zinc anodes. For construction, replace hydraulic filters.

Every 5,000 hours or 200,000 km: major overhaul â replace pistons, rings, bearings, and liners. This is expensive but extends life. Before that, do oil analysis every 250 hours to monitor wear.

Tools: keep a logbook. Use a grease gun, filter wrench, torque wrench, and multimeter. For oil changes, use a drain pan and funnel. Dispose of oil properly â never pour on ground.

In Africa, dust and heat accelerate wear. So shorten intervals by 20% if operating in dusty conditions. For example, change oil every 8,000 km instead of 10,000. Use high-quality filters â cheap ones fail. Also, train drivers to report unusual noises or smoke.

Finally, keep spare parts: oil filters, fuel filters, belts, hoses, and a spare impeller for marine. That way, you can do PM on time. A well-maintained engine can last 1,000,000 km. A neglected one fails at 200,000 km. The choice is yours.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Large Displacement Engines (6â12 Litres) in African Agribusiness and Transport

In African agribusiness, transport, and construction, engines between 6 and 12 litres are the workhorses that move harvests, building materials, and people. This practical reference distils the key specifications, maintenance intervals, and fuel strategies for heavy-duty truck and bus diesel engines, construction and mining equipment engines, marine diesel engines up to 12 litres, and high-performance petrol engines. It is written for fleet owners, workshop managers, and agripreneurs who need to keep equipment running profitably in dusty, hot, and remote conditions.

Whether you operate a 12-litre diesel truck hauling maize from the Rift Valley, a 6-litre excavator on a road project in Ghana, or a petrol-powered generator on a Kenyan flower farm, the principles of preventive maintenance and fuel efficiency are the same. The goal is simple: maximise uptime, minimise cost per tonne-kilometre or per hectare, and comply with tightening emission rules.

Engine Architecture and Duty Cycles

Large displacement engines are designed for continuous heavy loads. Diesel engines in this class typically use inline-six or V8 configurations, turbocharging, and high-pressure common-rail or unit injector fuel systems. Petrol engines of similar displacement are rarer but appear in high-performance pickups and gensets. In Africa, the most common 6â12 litre diesels are found in trucks (Mercedes-Benz Actros, Volvo FH, MAN TGS), buses (Scania, Yutong), construction equipment (Caterpillar, Komatsu, JCB), and marine applications (Yanmar, Cummins, Perkins).

Duty cycle matters. A truck on a paved highway may run at 60â80% load for hours, while an excavator cycles between 30% and 100% load with frequent idling. Marine engines often run at constant speed for long periods. Each duty cycle dictates different maintenance intervals and fuel strategies.

Heavy-Duty Truck and Bus Diesel Engines

In Africa, trucks and buses cover long distances on poor roads, often overloaded. Common engines include the Mercedes-Benz OM 470 (10.7 L), Volvo D11 (10.8 L), and Cummins ISL (8.9 L). These engines produce 300â450 hp and 1,200â2,200 Nm torque. Fuel consumption typically ranges from 25 to 40 L/100 km depending on load and terrain.

Key maintenance: oil and filter changes every 15,000â25,000 km or 500 hours; fuel filter every 20,000 km; air filter inspection every 10,000 km. In dusty conditions, intervals should be halved. Valve clearance adjustment every 100,000 km. Turbocharger inspection every 200,000 km.

Table 1: Typical maintenance intervals for 6â12 litre heavy-duty diesel engines in African conditions
Component Standard Interval African Dusty/Rough Road Interval Source
Engine oil & filter 20,000 km / 500 h 10,000 km / 250 h Cummins ISL Service Manual (2021)
Fuel filter 20,000 km 10,000 km Mercedes-Benz OM 470 Maintenance Sheet
Air filter 40,000 km 15,000 km Volvo D11 Operator's Manual
Valve clearance 100,000 km 60,000 km Bosch Automotive Handbook, 10th Ed.
Turbocharger inspection 200,000 km 120,000 km Caterpillar Diesel Engine Management Guide

Construction and Mining Equipment Engines

Excavators, loaders, and haul trucks use engines like the Caterpillar C7 (7.2 L), Komatsu SAA6D107E (6.7 L), and Cummins QSL9 (8.9 L). These engines operate in extreme dust, heat, and vibration. They often run at high idle for long periods, which dilutes oil and increases wear.

Maintenance focus: daily checks of air filter and coolant; oil changes every 250â500 hours; hydraulic oil every 2,000 hours; fuel system inspection every 1,000 hours. In mining, use of fuel with high sulphur content can damage aftertreatment systems. Where low-sulphur diesel is unavailable, consider engines without SCR or use fuel additives.

Marine Diesel Engines up to 12 Litres

Marine engines in this range power fishing boats, ferries, and river cargo vessels. Common models: Yanmar 6LY (5.8 L), Cummins QSB6.7 (6.7 L), Perkins M300C (7.0 L). They run at constant speed for hours, often in humid, salt-laden air. Corrosion and fuel contamination are major risks.

Maintenance: oil and filter every 250â500 hours; impeller replacement every 500 hours; fuel/water separator daily; coolant flush annually. In Africa, where fuel quality varies, install a secondary fuel filter and use biocide additives to prevent microbial growth in tanks.

High-Performance Petrol Engines

Petrol engines of 6â12 litres are rare but appear in high-performance pickups (e.g., Ford F-150 Raptor 3.5 L twin-turbo V6, not 6 L) and large generators. In agribusiness, petrol engines are common in smaller pumps and generators, but for 6â12 L, diesel dominates. However, some older petrol V8s (e.g., Toyota 1FZ-FE 4.5 L) are still used in Land Cruisers. For high-performance petrol, use high-octane fuel (95 RON minimum), change spark plugs every 40,000 km, and check ignition timing annually.

Fuel Efficiency and Emission Strategies

Fuel is the largest operating cost in African fleets, often 40â60% of total cost. Strategies to improve efficiency:

  • Driver training: smooth acceleration, correct gear selection, and avoiding excessive idling can cut fuel use by 10â15%.
  • Route optimisation: use GPS tracking to reduce empty running.
  • Regular maintenance: clogged filters and incorrect tyre pressure increase consumption.
  • Fuel quality: use low-sulphur diesel where available; otherwise, increase oil change frequency.
  • Aftertreatment: for Euro IIIâV engines, ensure DPF and SCR systems are functioning. In Africa, many vehicles are Euro II or older, so retrofitting is costly but may be required for urban access.
Table 2: Fuel efficiency and emission strategies for 6â12 litre engines in Africa

Low-sulphur diesel 0â2% Enables DPF/SCR, reduces SOx African Refiners Association (2020)

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: High-Pressure Fuel Systems

Modern common-rail diesel engines operate at pressures up to 2,500 bar (36,000 psi). Never loosen fuel lines while the engine is running. The high-pressure jet can penetrate skin and cause severe injury or death. Always depressurise the system according to the manufacturer's procedure before servicing. In African workshops, ensure only trained technicians work on these systems. Wear safety glasses and gloves. Keep a first-aid kit and emergency contact numbers visible.

Preventive Maintenance Schedules

A preventive maintenance (PM) schedule is the backbone of fleet reliability. In Africa, where spare parts may take weeks to arrive, PM is even more critical. Use the following as a template, then adjust for your specific engine and operating conditions.

  • Daily: Check oil level, coolant level, fuel/water separator, tyre pressure, and look for leaks.
  • Weekly: Inspect air filter restriction indicator, check battery terminals, drain water from fuel tank.
  • Monthly: Check belt tension, hoses, and clamps; test coolant concentration.
  • Every 250 hours / 10,000 km: Change engine oil and filter; inspect fuel filter.
  • Every 500 hours / 20,000 km: Replace fuel filter; check valve clearance (if applicable).
  • Every 1,000 hours / 40,000 km: Replace air filter; inspect turbocharger; check injectors.
  • Every 2,000 hours / 80,000 km: Replace coolant; inspect aftertreatment system; check EGR cooler.
  • Annually: Full engine diagnostic; replace timing belt (if equipped); clean DPF (if applicable).

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Daily: Oil, coolant, fuel/water separator, leaks, tyre pressure.
  • â Weekly: Air filter indicator, battery terminals, drain fuel water.
  • â Every 250 h: Engine oil and filter change.
  • â Every 500 h: Fuel filter change; valve clearance check.
  • â Every 1,000 h: Air filter change; turbo inspection.
  • â Every 2,000 h: Coolant flush; aftertreatment inspection.
  • â Fuel: Use low-sulphur diesel where possible; add biocide in marine tanks.
  • â Safety: Never open high-pressure fuel lines while running.

Further Reading

  • Cummins ISL Service Manual (PDF) â Official Cummins documentation for 8.9 L engines.
  • Mercedes-Benz Truck Operating Instructions â Free access to OM 470 and other engine manuals.
  • Volvo Trucks Operator Manuals â Downloadable manuals for D11 and D13 engines.
  • Caterpillar Maintenance Support â Guides for construction and mining engines.
  • Yanmar Marine Engine Manuals â Free downloads for marine diesel engines up to 12 L.

By following these practical guidelines, African agribusinesses and transport operators can extend engine life, reduce fuel costs, and meet emission standards. The key is consistency: daily checks, scheduled maintenance, and a safety-first culture. Invest in training and genuine parts, and your 6â12 litre engines will deliver reliable power for years.

quiz.q: What is the typical oil change interval for a Cummins ISX engine in heavy truck use?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states that a Cummins ISX needs oil changes every 15,000 km or 500 hours, whichever comes first.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to test diesel injectors?
quiz.explanation: A pop tester is used to test injector opening pressure and spray pattern.

quiz.q: What should you do if a truck engine overheats?
options: B) Check thermostat and radiator cap
quiz.explanation: The lesson advises checking the thermostat and radiator cap first when overheating.

quiz.q: For a Cummins ISX, what is the valve clearance for the intake valve on a cold engine?
quiz.explanation: The lesson specifies intake valve clearance of 0.30 mm for many models.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a clogged air filter in a diesel engine?
options: B) Black smoke and power loss
quiz.explanation: A clogged air filter causes black smoke and power loss due to rich mixture.

quiz.q: In construction equipment, how often should you take an oil sample for analysis?
quiz.explanation: The lesson recommends oil analysis every 250 hours for construction engines.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a water separator in a diesel fuel system?
options: B) To remove water from fuel
quiz.explanation: A water separator removes water, which can damage injectors.

quiz.q: When replacing a turbocharger, what should you do before starting the engine?
quiz.explanation: Pre-lubing the oil inlet with clean oil prevents turbo damage on start-up.

quiz.q: What is the maximum allowable side-to-side play in a turbocharger shaft?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states that if the shaft moves more than 0.1 mm side-to-side, replace the turbo.

quiz.q: For marine diesel engines, how often should the raw water pump impeller be replaced?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says replace the impeller every 500 hours or annually.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of zinc anodes in a marine heat exchanger?
quiz.explanation: Zinc anodes sacrifice themselves to protect the heat exchanger from corrosion.

quiz.q: What should you check if a marine diesel engine overheats at high RPM?
quiz.explanation: A clogged raw water strainer restricts cooling water flow, causing overheating.

quiz.q: What is the minimum compression for a 6-litre marine diesel engine?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states minimum compression is about 25 bar.

quiz.q: What type of fuel should high-performance petrol engines use?
quiz.explanation: High-performance petrol engines require high-octane fuel (95 RON or higher) to prevent knock.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spark plug gap for high-performance petrol engines?
quiz.explanation: The lesson specifies a gap of 1.1 mm for iridium or platinum plugs.

quiz.q: What is the target air/fuel ratio at wide-open throttle for best power?
quiz.explanation: The lesson recommends targeting 12.5:1 for best power.

quiz.q: What does a P0300 code indicate?
quiz.explanation: P0300 is a generic code for random or multiple cylinder misfire.

quiz.q: What is the torque specification for spark plugs in aluminium heads?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states to torque spark plugs to 25 Nm to avoid stripping aluminium threads.

quiz.q: How can you improve fuel efficiency by 10-15% on a truck?
options: B) Add roof fairing and side skirts
quiz.explanation: Aerodynamic aids like roof fairings and side skirts improve fuel economy by 10-15% at highway speeds.

quiz.q: What is the fuel saving from using low-viscosity engine oil?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states low-viscosity oil can save about 2% fuel.

quiz.q: What is the effect of a faulty O2 sensor on fuel consumption in a petrol engine?
quiz.explanation: A bad O2 sensor can increase fuel consumption by 15%.

quiz.q: What is the recommended daily check for a marine diesel engine?
quiz.explanation: Daily checks include checking the raw water strainer for debris.

quiz.q: How often should you change engine oil in a truck used in dusty conditions?
quiz.explanation: The lesson suggests shortening intervals by 20% in dusty conditions, so 10,000 km becomes 8,000 km, but the closest option is 10,000 km as a standard, but for dusty, it's 8,000 km. However, the lesson says 'change oil every 8,000 km instead of 10,000'. So the correct answer is not listed exactly. But based on the options, B is 10,000 km, which is the standard. The question asks for dusty conditions, so the answer should be 8,000 km. But since 8,000 is not an option, the closest is 10,000? Actually, the lesson says 'shorten intervals by 20%' so 10,000 * 0.8 = 8,000. So none of the options match exactly. I'll adjust the question to avoid confusion. Let me change the question: 'What is the standard oil change interval for a truck?' Then answer B. But I need to keep 30 questions. I'll rephrase: 'What is the standard oil change interval for a truck in normal conditions?' Answer B. So I'll change the question to that.
The lesson states oil changes every 10,000 km for trucks in normal conditions.

quiz.q: What is the first step in a daily preventive maintenance check?
quiz.explanation: Daily checks start with checking engine oil level, coolant, and fuel.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see black smoke from a diesel engine?
options: B) Check air filter and injectors
quiz.explanation: Black smoke indicates incomplete combustion, often from a clogged air filter or faulty injectors.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a thermostat in the cooling system?
quiz.explanation: The thermostat regulates coolant flow to maintain optimal engine temperature.

quiz.q: How often should you replace the fuel filter on a heavy-duty truck?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states fuel filters must be changed every 10,000 km.

quiz.q: What is the recommended coolant mix for African heat?
quiz.explanation: A 50/50 mix provides the best boil-over and freeze protection.

quiz.q: What should you check if a diesel engine cranks slowly?
quiz.explanation: Slow cranking is often due to a weak battery or poor earth connections.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of using a block heater in cold conditions?
quiz.explanation: A block heater warms the engine, making cold starts easier and reducing wear.
